title: Albert Alternatives for Budgeting and Cash Advances in 2026
h1: Albert Alternatives for Budgeting and Cash Advances in 2026
metaDescription: Albert alternatives compared: Monarch Money, YNAB, Simplifi, Copilot, Dave, Chime and EarnIn, with listed prices, advance limits and fees.
intro:
Monarch Money, YNAB, Quicken Simplifi and Copilot Money are four budgeting alternatives to [Albert](https://albert.com/), and Dave, Chime and EarnIn are three alternatives for early pay or cash advances. The pick depends on whether a budget tracker with a lower subscription matters most, or a cash advance with a small or no monthly fee. The table lists each provider's published prices and limits, and the sections below turn those prices into yearly totals.

Albert calls itself "the all-in-one money app" and says over 10 million customers trust it. Its subscription plans range from $19.99 to $39.99 per month, with 30 days to try a plan before the first charge. Albert also offers Genius, an artificial intelligence (AI) financial assistant that creates a budget automatically from spending and categorizes transactions.

Albert is not a bank. Stride Bank, N.A., Member Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), provides the banking services behind the Albert Cash debit account, which lists fee-free automated teller machines (ATMs). Albert's Instant Advance runs from $25 to $1,000 at Albert's discretion, with no late fees, no interest and no Albert subscription required.

On the cash side, Chime lists savings up to 4.00% annual percentage yield (APY) and Early Payday with no mandatory fees. EarnIn lists Cash Out with no mandatory fees, no interest and no credit check.

For wider shortlists, see the [best budgeting apps roundup](/roundup/best-budgeting-apps/), the [how to make a budget guide](/guides/how-to-make-a-budget/), [Monarch Money alternatives](/alternatives/monarch-money/), [YNAB alternatives](/alternatives/ynab/) and [Dave alternatives](/alternatives/dave/). The [comparison hub](/compare/) collects more side-by-side pages.

chooseSection.heading: How to Choose an Albert Alternative
chooseSection.body:
Each Albert alternative covers one side of what Albert bundles, so the first choice is between budgeting and early cash. Monarch Money, YNAB, Quicken Simplifi and Copilot Money list budgeting with no bank account or cash advance on the pages checked. Dave, Chime and EarnIn list early pay or advances, and of those three only Dave lists a Goals account for tracking savings.

Compare three things before picking.

- Yearly cost. Albert's plans at $19.99 a month total $239.88 a year, and at $39.99 a month they total $479.88. Every budgeting alternative here lists an annual price below $239.88, from $47.88 for Quicken Simplifi to $199.99 for Monarch Plus.
- Advance size and fees. Albert's Instant Advance and EarnIn's Cash Out each reach $1,000, Chime's Early Payday reaches $750 and Dave's ExtraCash reaches $500. Dave adds a monthly membership of up to $5, while Chime and EarnIn list no mandatory fees.
- Where the money sits. Albert, Dave and Chime each name partner banks for FDIC insurance. EarnIn's home page shows no bank account.

A reader who wants both budgeting and early cash can pair one app from each group. Quicken Simplifi at $47.88 a year plus Dave at up to $60 a year totals up to $107.88, which is $132.00 less than Albert's $239.88 low plan. Quicken Simplifi paired with EarnIn's standard Cash Out costs $47.88 a year, because EarnIn lists no mandatory fees.

Albert's advances work without a plan. Instant Advance and the Instant Line of Credit need no Albert subscription, so a reader who only wants an Albert advance pays no plan fee. Transfers within minutes may carry a transfer fee, and the line of credit has draw fees.

alternatives.heading: Monarch Money Core and Plus Pricing
alternatives.body:
Monarch Money is a budgeting app with two plans. Core costs $99.99 per year or $14.99 per month, and Plus costs $199.99 per year. Plus adds forecasting tools, tracking for multiple income sources like a small business, and deeper investment tracking.

Monarch Money says it shows no ads and never sells financial data. Monarch recommends signing up on the web rather than through app stores, and the first week is free. Plans can be canceled anytime, and Monarch lists a money-back guarantee.

Monarch Money fits people who want budgeting without ads and who need no bank account or cash advance from the same provider. Neither a bank account nor a cash advance appears on the Monarch pricing page.

A year of Core on monthly billing costs $14.99 x 12 = $179.88, against $99.99 on annual billing, a gap of $79.89. Albert's lowest plan at $19.99 a month costs $239.88 a year, which is $139.89 more than Core billed annually. Monarch Plus at $199.99 a year comes in $39.89 below Albert's lowest plan.

Both providers list a planning feature. Monarch puts forecasting tools on Plus, and Albert lists Forecast for planning big expenses months ahead without saying which of its plans includes it.

alternatives.heading: YNAB Annual Plan and Free Trial
alternatives.body:
YNAB is a budgeting app built around giving every dollar a job. The annual plan costs $109 per year, which YNAB shows as $9.08 per month, and the monthly plan costs $14.99 per month, plus tax where applicable. YNAB connects accounts and offers a 34-day free trial with no credit card required.

YNAB fits people who want a budgeting method that gives every dollar a job. YNAB lists no bank account or cash advance on its pricing page.

A year of monthly billing costs $14.99 x 12 = $179.88, which is $70.88 more than the $109 annual plan. Albert's $19.99 low plan totals $239.88 a year, or $130.88 more than YNAB billed annually. The YNAB trial runs 34 days, four days longer than Albert's 30-day plan trial.

The two approaches start from different places. Albert's Genius creates a budget automatically from spending, while YNAB's method centers on giving every dollar a job. Albert's disclosure says Genius can make mistakes and is not a financial advisor.

alternatives.heading: Quicken Simplifi Spending Plan and Price
alternatives.body:
Quicken Simplifi lists the lowest budgeting price among these Albert alternatives at $3.99 per month billed annually, and the same page also shows $6.99. Simplifi runs on mobile and web. It links bank, credit card, loan and investment accounts at over 14,000 financial institutions.

The Spending Plan takes bills, subscriptions and savings out first, and what is left is for spending or saving. Projected Cash Flow maps balances up to 12 months ahead, which gives a year-long view of where balances are heading.

Quicken Simplifi fits people who want the lowest listed yearly cost for budgeting and a forward view of balances. No bank account or cash advance appears on the Simplifi page.

At $3.99 per month billed annually, Simplifi costs $47.88 a year. Albert's $19.99 low plan costs $192.00 more per year, and Albert's $39.99 plan costs $432.00 more. Albert connects to thousands of institutions, and Simplifi lists over 14,000.

alternatives.heading: Copilot Money Single Plan Pricing
alternatives.body:
Copilot Money sells one plan at $109 billed yearly, listed as $9 per month and marked down from $119. Copilot says there are no tiers, no add-ons and no AI credits, and everyone gets the full experience. The monthly billing price does not appear in the Copilot page text.

Copilot connects to 16,000+ institutions and runs on iPhone, iPad, Mac and web, with support from real humans. Its money assistant asks before acting. Copilot says it never sells financial data and lists 4.8 stars from 31,000+ ratings.

Copilot lists partner invites as "coming this fall". Copilot Money fits people on Apple devices or the web who want one price with every feature included. No bank account or cash advance appears on the Copilot page.

Albert's $19.99 low plan costs $239.88 a year, which is $130.88 more than Copilot's $109. Copilot lists one price for everything, while Albert lists a $19.99 to $39.99 range without publishing which features come at each price.

alternatives.heading: Dave ExtraCash Limits and Membership Fee
alternatives.body:
Dave offers ExtraCash from $25 to $500, typically authorized within 5 minutes. Dave lists no credit check, interest or late fees, and ExtraCash is repayable on demand. Not all members qualify, and few qualify for $500.

ExtraCash carries an overdraft fee equal to the greater of $5 or 5%. On a $500 ExtraCash, 5% is $25, which is greater than $5. An optional 1.5% fee applies to external debit card transfers, so a $500 transfer to an outside debit card would cost $7.50.

Dave charges a monthly membership fee of up to $5 for ExtraCash, Income Opportunity Services and Financial Management Services, which is up to $60 a year. Using ExtraCash requires opening an ExtraCash overdraft deposit account and a Dave Checking account.

Dave Checking pays up to 2 days early, and a Goals account tracks savings. Deposits are FDIC insured up to $250,000 through Coastal Community Bank, Member FDIC, or another partner bank, with conditions. Dave says it has 14M+ members, and its CashAI analyzes 180+ data points, including income, gig or irregular work, bank balance and spending patterns.

Dave fits people who want an advance with no credit check and a membership fee of up to $5 a month. Albert's Instant Advance reaches $1,000 and needs no subscription, while Dave's ExtraCash tops out at $500.

alternatives.heading: Chime Early Payday and SpotMe Overdraft
alternatives.body:
Chime is a fintech with fee-free banking. Chime is not a bank, and FDIC insurance comes through The Bancorp Bank, N.A. and Stride Bank, N.A., with conditions. Stride Bank, N.A. is also the bank Albert names for its banking services.

Early Payday gives access to up to $750 of pay with no mandatory fees and no interest, through a MyPay line of credit from The Bancorp Bank, N.A. or Stride Bank, N.A. Optional services may carry fees, such as outbound instant transfers and out-of-network ATM use. With direct deposit, a paycheck can arrive up to two days early.

SpotMe covers overdrafts up to $20 at first, with later eligibility for $200 or more based on account history and direct deposits, and no fee on debit. Chime lists 47K fee-free ATMs. Savings earn up to 4.00% APY, a variable rate that can change at any time, with higher rates tied to Chime Prime with qualifying direct deposits.

Chime Plus and Chime Prime pay 2% and 5% cash back on up to $1,500 of eligible secured credit card purchases with qualifying direct deposits. On $1,500 of those purchases, that is $30 on Plus and $75 on Prime.

Chime fits people who want a fee-free account with early pay access and SpotMe overdraft cover. Chime's home page shows no budgeting or net worth tracker, while Albert lists net worth tracking and a weekly spending report.

alternatives.heading: EarnIn Cash Out and Early Pay Fees
alternatives.body:
EarnIn Cash Out gives access to up to $200 a day and $1,000 per pay period, with no mandatory fees, no interest and no credit check. Limits vary by user eligibility. Standard transfers usually take 1 to 2 business days.

Tips are optional and do not affect service. An optional Lightning Speed fee buys faster delivery than the standard 1 to 2 business days.

Early Pay moves direct deposits up to 2 days sooner for $2.99, so using it 12 times in a year would cost $35.88. Live Pay gives real-time access to pay, up to $1,500 per pay period. Balance Shield sends low-balance alerts.

EarnIn fits people who want access to earned pay with no mandatory fee on standard Cash Out. EarnIn's home page shows no budgeting app or bank account. Albert's Instant Advance and EarnIn's per-pay-period Cash Out both top out at $1,000.

stillBetterFit.heading: When Albert Is the Better Fit
stillBetterFit.body:
Albert fits people who want budgeting, a debit account, savings, investing and identity protection from one provider. Albert lists automatic categorization, spending and cash flow tracking, a weekly spending report, bill increase alerts, bill lowering negotiation, subscription cancellation and net worth tracking. Albert Cash adds cash back on spend and early pay with direct deposit.

Investing covers stocks, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and strategies managed by Albert, with advisory services by Albert Investments, LLC, a Registered Investment Advisor, and brokerage by Albert Securities, LLC. Securities are not FDIC insured and may lose value. Cash and Savings funds are eligible for up to $250,000 of FDIC insurance on a pass-through basis, subject to conditions.

Identity protection includes 24/7 monitoring, dark web monitoring, credit report alerts, fraud alerts, online data privacy and up to $1M of identity theft insurance. Albert's two advance products need no subscription: Instant Advance and the Instant Line of Credit from FinWise Bank both run from $25 to $1,000.

Who this is not for:

- People who only want a budget tracker. Albert's lowest plan costs $239.88 a year, and Quicken Simplifi lists $47.88 a year.
- People who want High Yield Savings without a subscription. Albert requires an eligible subscription tier for it, and Albert says its fees may reduce earnings; Chime lists fee-free banking with savings up to 4.00% APY.
- People who need more than $1,000 of pay access in one pay period. EarnIn Live Pay lists up to $1,500 per pay period.
- People who want a fixed price that covers every feature. Albert does not publish which features come at which price, and Copilot Money lists one plan at $109 a year with no tiers.

What would change our answer:

- Albert publishing a per-plan feature list for its $19.99 to $39.99 range.
- Albert pricing its lowest plan below Monarch Core's $99.99 a year or Copilot Money's $109 a year.
- Albert requiring a subscription for Instant Advance or the Instant Line of Credit.
- Copilot Money launching the partner invites it lists as "coming this fall".
- Dave changing its up to $5 monthly membership or its greater-of-$5-or-5% overdraft fee.
- EarnIn adding a mandatory fee to standard Cash Out, or Chime adding one to Early Payday.

verdict:
Quicken Simplifi lists the lowest yearly budgeting cost at $47.88, and Monarch Money Core, YNAB and Copilot Money each list $99.99 to $109 a year, all below Albert's $239.88 low plan. For early cash, EarnIn and Chime list no mandatory fees on standard Cash Out and Early Payday, and Dave charges up to $5 a month. Albert fits people who want budgeting, banking, investing and identity protection together, and its Instant Advance of up to $1,000 needs no subscription.

To narrow these Albert alternatives, write down whether budgeting or early cash comes first and the yearly amount available for a subscription, then match both to the rows in the table above.

faqs.question: Does Albert charge a monthly fee?
faqs.answer: Yes, for its subscription plans. Albert's plans range from $19.99 to $39.99 a month, with 30 days to try a plan before the first charge, and plans auto-renew until canceled in the Albert app. Instant Advance and the Instant Line of Credit do not require an Albert subscription.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest app like Albert?
faqs.answer: Quicken Simplifi lists the lowest price among the budgeting alternatives at $3.99 a month billed annually, or $47.88 a year. Monarch Money Core lists $99.99 a year, and YNAB and Copilot Money each list $109 a year. For early cash, EarnIn and Chime list no mandatory fees on standard Cash Out and Early Payday.

faqs.question: Does Albert require a subscription for cash advances?
faqs.answer: No. Albert says an Albert subscription is not required to use Instant Advance, which runs from $25 to $1,000 at Albert's discretion. Transfers to an external account within minutes may carry a transfer fee, and the Instant Line of Credit has draw fees.

faqs.question: Is Albert a bank?
faqs.answer: No. Albert says it is not a bank, and Stride Bank, N.A., Member FDIC, provides its banking services. Cash and Savings funds are eligible for up to $250,000 of FDIC insurance on a pass-through basis, subject to conditions.

faqs.question: Which Albert alternative has no mandatory fees?
faqs.answer: EarnIn lists no mandatory fees for standard Cash Out, and Chime lists no mandatory fees for Early Payday. Dave charges a membership fee of up to $5 a month. EarnIn's Lightning Speed fee and Chime's outbound instant transfer fee are optional.

faqs.question: Which Albert alternative is best for budgeting only?
faqs.answer: Monarch Money, YNAB, Quicken Simplifi and Copilot Money are the budgeting-only alternatives, and none lists a cash advance or bank account on the pages checked. Simplifi lists the lowest yearly cost at $47.88, YNAB offers a 34-day free trial with no credit card, and Copilot Money sells one plan with no tiers.
